reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it presents a OneCoin cryptocurrency pitch that asks viewers to invest, sign up, and make a purchase through a OneCoin URL. The speaker claims value grows as more people join and promotes paid package tiers, including a 5000-euro package, while linking purchase level and personal-data submission to claimed Mastercard benefits. The presentation solicits participation based on network-value and usability claims, although it does not establish card issuance, URL behavior, losses, or authorization of claimed affiliations.

opening.argument: The speaker expressly tempers expectations rather than presenting an immediate or guaranteed result: “don't expect it to be from today to tomorrow” and “It is a slow process.” The discussion also acknowledges that cryptocurrency has no inherent value and explains value as something dependent on use and adoption, which is analysis of a volatile technology rather than a promise of returns. A careful viewer could reasonably understand this as a qualified presentation that describes uncertainty and rollout limitations, not deceptive certainty.

citations.quote: I want to warn you don't expect it to be from today to tomorrow. It is a slow process.
In and of itself it has no value at all. Nothing!
Just because I can buy and sell something, it has absolutely no value.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The purchase language and package comparison show that OneCoin was being discussed commercially, but they do not establish a guaranteed return or concealment of risk. The cited network-value statement is a theory about how cryptocurrency adoption may affect value, while the presentation also expressly cautions that rollout is slow. The Mastercard passage describes processing, not a guaranteed financial benefit.

citations.quote: cryptocurrency is actually one of the few products that really become valuable the more people get in
I want to warn you don't expect it to be from today to tomorrow. It is a slow process.
it will just take still four or six weeks to process everything

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The caution concerns timing, not the possibility of losing money or the reliability of the product. The speaker still links value to additional participation and discusses a 5000-euro package. Saying cryptocurrency has no inherent value does not neutralize an appeal to buy it; it can instead make adoption claims the central reason viewers are asked to participate.

opening.argument: The material can be read as an educational presentation explaining cryptocurrency to a general audience, not as a direct fraud solicitation. The speaker says the audience should understand what cryptocurrency is even if they cannot explain blockchain in detail, then compares Bitcoin, gold, brands, networks, payment use, and card usability. She also recounts a failed or impractical Bitcoin-card experience, including that she “had no chance to use it,” which is commentary and demonstration of limitations rather than a certification that every crypto claim is true.

citations.quote: they should still understand what is a cryptocurrency
Perhaps none of you would know how to explain blockchain in detail

they can't really get in and go shopping something which is interesting for the mass market

rebuttal.rebuttal: The educational format does not change what the presentation tells viewers to do. Its description explicitly instructs viewers to invest, sign up, and purchase, and the talk explains why OneCoin should become more valuable as participation grows. Teaching terminology can make a commercial pitch more persuasive; it does not by itself make the underlying offer ordinary or neutral.

citations.quote: Invest in OneCoin cryptocurrency, sign up and make your purchase
cryptocurrency is actually one of the few products that really become valuable the more people get in

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The educational framing is inseparable from promotion: the explanation repeatedly presents OneCoin as the accessible successor to Bitcoin and connects its value to a growing network. The anecdote about an unusable Bitcoin card criticizes a competing implementation, but it does not show that OneCoin itself worked or that its claimed usability was independently demonstrated.

opening.argument: The supplied material describes a commercial product and proposed payment service, but does not establish the core mechanics of a scam. The description gives a purchase and signup route, while the presentation discusses a branded Mastercard, identity processing, and eventual use for goods and payments. It does not state a guaranteed return, a required downline, or a promised income outcome. In fact, the speaker says processing takes four to six weeks and that rollout is gradual, which is more consistent with an ordinary service claim whose safety and performance remain unverified than with proof of a fraudulent mechanism.

I can do it with the coins and use them wherever I go and I will spend all this coins.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The fact that a purchase route exists does not prove that the service is a scam, and the cited package amount is a price distinction rather than evidence of a promised payout. The Mastercard excerpt says that people who submit documents are able to get one, but the supplied material does not establish whether issuance occurred, whether the card worked, or whether users were guaranteed any benefit.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The missing proof of a completed card is not a defense when the presentation uses the proposed utility to encourage purchase. It also explicitly says that OneCoin becomes valuable as more people join, so the issue is not merely a neutral retail price. The absence of a quoted guarantee does not remove the appreciation-based solicitation or establish ordinary commerce.
